# Essential yet limited role for CCR2+ inflammatory monocytes during Mycobacterium tuberculosis-specific T cell priming

## Authors

- Miriam Samstein<sup>1</sup> †
- Heidi A Schreiber<sup>4</sup>
- Ingrid M Leiner<sup>1</sup>
- Bože Sušac<sup>1</sup>
- Michael S Glickman<sup>1</sup>
- Eric G Pamer<sup>1</sup> †

### Affiliations

1. Program in Immunology and Microbial Pathogenesis Weill Cornell Graduate School of Medical Sciences New York United States
2. Infectious Disease Service, Department of Medicine Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center New York United States
3. Weill Cornell, Rockefeller, Sloan-Kettering Tri-Institutional MD-PhD Program New York United States
4. Laboratory of Molecular Immunology The Rockefeller University New York United States

† Corresponding author

## Abstract

10.7554/eLife.01086.001 Defense against infection by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) is mediated by CD4 T cells. CCR2 + inflammatory monocytes (IMs) have been implicated in Mtb-specific CD4 T cell responses but their in vivo contribution remains unresolved. Herein, we show that transient ablation of IMs during infection prevents Mtb delivery to pulmonary lymph nodes, reducing CD4 T cell responses. Transfer of MHC class II-expressing IMs to MHC class II-deficient, monocyte-depleted recipients, while restoring Mtb transport to mLNs, does not enable Mtb-specific CD4 T cell priming. On the other hand, transfer of MHC class II-deficient IMs corrects CD4 T cell priming in monocyte-depleted, MHC class II-expressing mice. Specific depletion of classical DCs does not reduce Mtb delivery to pulmonary lymph nodes but markedly reduces CD4 T cell priming. Thus, although IMs acquire characteristics of DCs while delivering Mtb to lymph nodes, cDCs but not moDCs induce proliferation of Mtb-specific CD4 T cells. DOI: http://dx.doi.org/10.7554/eLife.01086.001

## Introduction

Inflammatory monocytes (IMs) express Ly6c, CD11b and CCR2, a chemokine receptor that facilitates emigration of IMs from the bone marrow (Serbina and Pamer, 2006). Although IMs make important contributions to innate immune defense during infection, recent studies also implicate IMs in priming of CD4 T cell responses during fungal, viral and parasitic infections (Traynor et al., 2000; Leon et al., 2007; Edismo et al., 2009; Hohl et al., 2009; Rivera et al., 2011). Experiments using CCR2-deficient mice also suggested that monocytes contribute to T-cell-mediated defense against Mtb. IMs, however, can also serve as permissive host cells for Mtb in later stages of infection, suggesting that IMs can both restrict and enhance Mtb infection (Antonelli et al., 2010). Because recruitment of IMs in CCR2-deficient mice is defective throughout early, intermediate and late stages of infection, it has not been possible to specifically define the role of monocytes at different times during infection (Peters et al., 2001; Scott and Flynn, 2002; Peters et al., 2004). Therefore, we used CCR2-DTR mice to transiently deplete IMs and other CCR2-expressing cells during discrete stages of Mtb infection.

Although IMs represent the most prevalent CCR2-expressing cell population, subsets of NK cells, dendritic cells and CD4 T cells can also express CCR2. To exclude the possibility that depletion of a non-monocyte cell population resulted in loss of Mtb transport from lungs to mLNs, we purified IMs from CCR2-GFP mice by sorting GFP+ cells that did not express NK1.1, CD4, FLT3 and C-kit. This strategy did not require antibody staining for trafficking molecules (CCR2 and CD11b) and eliminated NK cells, CD4 T cells, dendritic cell progenitors and hematopoietic stem cells, yielding a highly purified (>99% pure) population of IMs (

![Figure 3.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/01086/elife-01086-fig3-v1.jpg)

(A) Mice were euthanized on day 12 post infection and flow cytometry was performed on lungs and mLNs to track the engraftment of adoptively transferred IMs. (B) The expression of cell surface markers CD11b, MHC II, CDIIc and CD103 by adoptively transferred IMs in the lung and mLN was determined. (C) CFU plots from day 12 mLNs of CCR2-DTR mice rescued with IMs. Dots marked in red represent mice that received double sorted IMs of greater than 99% purity. (D) CCR2-DTR mice received a dose of naive ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells the day before infection and were treated with DT on days 7, 9 and 11 and received purified IMs or PBS on days 8 and 10. Lungs were harvested on day 15 and ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells were visualized. (E) Cumulative data of experiment shown in (D) showing the total number of ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells in day 15 lungs. (F) CCR2-DTR mice were depleted on days 7, 9 and 11 and received CCR2 WT or CCR2 KO IMs on days 8 and 10. Day 12 mLNs were harvested for CFU counts. Each dot represents an individual mouse. Error bars denote SEM. Data are representative of two independent experiments.DOI: http://dx.doi.org/10.7554/eLife.01086.006

![Figure 3—figure supplement 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/01086/elife-01086-fig3-figsupp1-v1.jpg)

While the CCR2 chemokine receptor is required for egress of IMs from bone marrow (Serbina and Pamer, 2006), the role of CCR2 in trafficking of IMs into infected lungs or from the sites of lung infection to draining lymph nodes remains incompletely resolved. To determine whether CCR2 is required for trafficking to lungs and mLNs during Mtb infection, we purified IMs from CCR2-deficient, CCR2-GFP mice for adoptive transfer into Mtb-infected, CCR2-DTR recipient mice that were monocyte depleted between 7 and 11 days following infection. Quantitative culture 12 days following Mtb infection demonstrated that wild-type and CCR2-deficient IMs were equivalent at delivering Mtb to mLNs, indicating that CCR2-signaling does not contribute to trafficking of IMs between these sites (Figure 3F).

Although IMs acquired characteristics of dendritic cells and are essential for Mtb transport from infected lungs to mLNs, it remained unclear whether IMs directly primed Mtb-specific CD4 T cells. Therefore, we transferred C7 T cells into MHC class II-deficient CCR2-DTR mice, depleted monocytes 7–11 days following infection and adoptively transferred MHC class II-expressing purified monocytes on days 8 and 10 following infection. In contrast to our previous experiments with MHC class II-expressing recipients, C7 T cells were not primed in MHC class II-deficient recipients of MHC class II-expressing monocytes (

Classical DCs in lymph nodes and their progenitors express the cDC-specific transcription factor zbtb46, whereas IMs do not. To determine whether classical DCs are required for Mtb-specific CD4 T cell priming, we used zDC-DTR mice, in which DT administration leads to a loss of classical DC populations (Meredith et al., 2012a; Meredith et al., 2012b). We transferred C7 T cells into zDC-DTR mice, infected the mice with Mtb and administered DT on days 7–11 following infection. Depletion of classical DCs resulted in markedly reduced C7 T cell expansion (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2) but did not reduce the number of live Mtb in mLNs (Figure 4E). FLT3L-deficient mice, which lack classical DCs but not IMs, also have markedly reduced CD4 T cell responses following Mtb infection (Figure 4F) despite the presence of Mtb in the mLN (Figure 4—figure supplement 3). These results indicate that classical DCs, while dispensable for trafficking of live Mtb from infected lungs to mLNs, are essential for CD4 T cell priming.

These experiments have refined our understanding of the role of IMs during the initiation of adaptive immune defense against M. tuberculosis infection. During the second week of murine infection, IMs play the critical role of delivering live Mtb to draining mLNs, an indispensable step for Mtb-specific CD4 T cell priming. Our results extend previous reports that IMs influence CD4 T cell priming (Leon et al., 2007; Hohl et al., 2009; Nakano et al., 2009; Rivera et al., 2011) by demonstrating that IMs serve as transporters of live bacteria from the site of infection to the site of T cell priming.

In contrast to reports from other disease models demonstrating that IMs differentiate into DCs and then directly prime CD4 T cells (Cheong et al., 2010; Zigmond et al., 2012) our adoptive transfer studies using MHC class II KO mice reveal that IMs, despite acquiring characteristics of DCs, do not prime Mtb-specific CD4 T cells in vivo. Why IMs fail to prime DCs in this setting remains unclear. Evidence that moDCs generated in vitro can stimulate T cell responses suggests that IMs can process and present antigen (Schreurs et al., 1999). Recovery of several hundred adoptively transferred IMs from the mLNs of infected mice also suggests that sufficient numbers of IM were present to prime T cells. One possible explanation is that IMs, by virtue of being infected with Mtb, are ineffective at stimulating Mtb-specific lymphocytes, in contrast to resident dendritic cells that have not been infected (Wolf et al., 2007).

Antigen transport and T cell priming are often considered the two major functions of DCs. A number of studies, however, have demonstrated that multiple DC subsets can be involved in priming of naive T cells (Itano et al., 2003). Other studies characterizing CD8 T cell responses to cutaneous viral infection have demonstrated a role for CD103+ DCs in transport and priming with potential contributions by inflammatory monocytes (Bedoui et al., 2009; Edismo et al., 2009). One previous study has suggested that IMs carry fungal antigens from a site of cutaneous inoculation to draining LNs and transfer antigens to LN resident DCs (Ersland et al., 2010). Our study extends this finding to live pulmonary infection with Mtb. IMs transport bacteria to lymph nodes and transfer antigen to classical dendritic cells prior to CD4 T cell priming.

The mechanism of antigen transfer in mLNs remains undefined. It is possible that cross-dressing (Wakim et al., 2011), in which infected cells pass MHC molecules to uninfected cells, plays a role during Mtb infection. We did not detect transfer of MHC class II molecules from host cells to adoptively transferred, MHC class II-deficient monocytes. The number of MHC/peptide complexes required per APC to stimulate T cell responses, however, may be very small and below our level of detection. That said, given our finding that MHC class II-deficient IMs effectively complemented monocyte-depleted, MHC class II sufficient mice while MHC class II-expressing monocytes could not correct deficient T cell priming in MHC class II-deficient, monocyte-depleted mice, we believe that transfer of MHC class II molecules in either direction plays a minimal role in T cell priming during Mtb infection. Future studies will determine whether live Mtb are transferred to classical DCs, or whether transfer principally involves the movement of processed or unprocessed proteins from infected monocytes to uninfected DCs.

## Materials and methods

## Mice

C57BL/6 and MHC class II-deficient mice were purchased from the Jackson Laboratory. The generation of ESAT-6-specific C7 TCR transgenic, CCR2-DTR, CCR2-GFP and zDC-DTR mice were previously described (Wolf et al., 2007; Gallegos et al., 2008; Hohl et al., 2009). For depletion experiments, mice were injected i.p. with 20 ng/g body weight DT. All mice were bred and maintained under specific pathogen-free conditions at the Memorial Sloan Kettering Research Animal Resource Center. Sex-and age-matched controls were used in all experiments according to institutional guidelines for animal care. All animal procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center.

## Aerosol infections with M. tuberculosis

M. tuberculosis Erdman was grown in 7H9 media, and log phase cultures were diluted to 8 × 106 bacilli per millimeter and sonicated before infection with an aerosol exposure system (Glass-Col). The volume of suspension, and exposure time were calibrated to deliver ∼100 CFU per animal. To determine infection dose, three mice were killed 1 day after infection and lungs were homogenized in PBS/0.05% Tween-80, and half the lung homogenate was plated. At various intervals after infection the left lung was harvested from individual mice and homogenized in PBS/0.05% Tween-80. Serial dilutions were made in PBS/0.05% Tween-80 and plated onto Middlebrook 7H10 agar (BD Biosciences). After 3 weeks of incubation at 37°C in a 5% CO2 atmosphere, colonies were counted.

## Adoptive IM transfer

Inflammatory monocytes were harvested from the bone marrow of CCR2-GFP mice. CD4 T cells and NK+ cells were removed using antibody depletion kits from Miltenyi Biotec. The remaining cells were then stained with anti FLT3 PE and anti C-kit PE antibodies and EGFP+, PE- cells were sorted by the Memorial Sloan-Kettering Cancer Center flow cytometry core facility. The cells were re-suspended in PBS and 2 × 10 (Kipnis et al., 2003) cells per mouse were injected via the tail vein.

## Statistics

All data are presented as the arithmetic mean ± SEM. Statistical validation was done with the Student’s t test. p<0.05 were considered significant, p>0.05 were considered insignificant.

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.01086.012](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.01086.012)

eLife posts the editorial decision letter and author response on a selection of the published articles (subject to the approval of the authors). An edited version of the letter sent to the authors after peer review is shown, indicating the substantive concerns or comments; minor concerns are not usually shown. Reviewers have the opportunity to discuss the decision before the letter is sent (see review process). Similarly, the author response typically shows only responses to the major concerns raised by the reviewers.

Thank you for sending your work entitled “Essential yet limited role for CCR2+ inflammatory monocytes during Mycobacterium tuberculosis-specific T cell priming” for consideration at eLife. Your article has been favorably evaluated by a Senior editor and 2 reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors.

The Reviewing editor and the other reviewer discussed their comments before we reached this decision, and the Reviewing editor has assembled the following comments to help you prepare a revised submission.

This is an elegant and straightforward study that makes an important contribution on the role of different APCs in transport and presentation of antigen in vivo in a biologically relevant system.

The only open aspect is the mechanism of antigen transfer from inflammatory monocytes to resident DC. It would be interesting if the authors could provide insights on why the monocytes that carry Mtb to lymph nodes do not present antigen to CD4+ T cells. Is there a problem with their localization within lymph nodes? Or are they incompetent for antigen processing and presentation (their antigen presentation capacity could be tested ex vivo)? Or are they too few to function as APC and their role is limited to spreading a live organism? In addition the authors may also consider the alternative possibility that resident DCs transfer their MHC class II molecules to inflammatory monocytes (a process related to “cross dressing”). In this case DC depletion would block T cell activation because the source of MHC class II is absent. This possibility could be addressed by asking whether there is any MHC class II on class II KO inflammatory monocytes after adoptive transfer and infection. While these experiments would provide a mechanistic explanation to the results, they are not essential to support the major conclusions of the study and consequently the authors may address these issues in the Discussion.

claims.evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Adoptively transferred IMs engraft in lungs and mLNs of CCR2-DTR mice.
claims.source: CCR2-DTR mice were infected and treated with DT or PBS on days 7, 9 and 11 and received highly purified CD45.1+ IMs on days 8 and 10. (A) Mice were euthanized on day 12 post infection and flow cytometry was performed on lungs and mLNs to track the engraftment of adoptively transferred IMs.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A where transferred IMs are detected in lungs and mLNs.

claims.claim: Adoptively transferred IMs in the lung and mLN express CD11b, MHC II, CD11c and CD103.
claims.source: The expression of cell surface markers CD11b, MHC II, CDIIc and CD103 by adoptively transferred IMs in the lung and mLN was determined.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B by flow cytometry analysis.

claims.claim: Transfer of purified IMs to DT-treated CCR2-DTR mice restores Mtb CFU in mLNs on day 12.
claims.source: CFU plots from day 12 mLNs of CCR2-DTR mice rescued with IMs.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C where IM transfer restores CFU levels in mLNs.

claims.claim: Transfer of purified IMs to DT-treated CCR2-DTR mice increases ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells in lungs on day 15.
claims.source: CCR2-DTR mice received a dose of naive ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells the day before infection and were treated with DT on days 7, 9 and 11 and received purified IMs or PBS on days 8 and 10. Lungs were harvested on day 15 and ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells were visualized.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D and 3E where IM transfer increases C7 T cell numbers.

claims.claim: CCR2-signaling does not contribute to trafficking of IMs between lungs and mLNs during Mtb infection.
claims.source: Quantitative culture 12 days following Mtb infection demonstrated that wild-type and CCR2-deficient IMs were equivalent at delivering Mtb to mLNs, indicating that CCR2-signaling does not contribute to trafficking of IMs between these sites (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3F showing equivalent Mtb delivery by WT and CCR2 KO IMs.

claims.claim: Wild-type and CCR2-deficient IMs are equivalent at delivering Mtb to mLNs.
claims.source: Quantitative culture 12 days following Mtb infection demonstrated that wild-type and CCR2-deficient IMs were equivalent at delivering Mtb to mLNs
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3F by CFU analysis.

claims.claim: C7 T cells were not primed in MHC class II-deficient recipients of MHC class II-expressing monocytes.
claims.source: In contrast to our previous experiments with MHC class II-expressing recipients, C7 T cells were not primed in MHC class II-deficient recipients of MHC class II-expressing monocytes
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A where MHC II KO mice receiving MHC II+ IMs do not show C7 T cell expansion.

claims.claim: Transfer of MHC class II-expressing IMs to MHC class II-deficient, monocyte-depleted recipients restores Mtb CFU in mLNs.
claims.source: Mtb CFUs from mLNs of mice harvested on day 12.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B where MHC II KO mice receiving IMs have restored CFU levels.

claims.claim: Transfer of MHC class II WT or MHC class II KO IMs to DT-treated CCR2-DTR mice results in similar ESAT-6-specific C7 T cell expansion in lungs on day 15.
claims.source: CCR2-DTR mice received naive ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells the day before infection and were treated with DT or PBS on days 7, 9 and 11 and received either MHCII WT or MHCII KO IMs on days 8 and 10. Flow cytometry was performed on lungs harvested on day 15.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C where both MHC II WT and KO IMs restore C7 T cell responses.

claims.claim: Depletion of classical DCs on days 7, 9 and 11 reduces ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells in mLNs on day 12.
claims.source: zDC-DTR mice received naive ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells the day before infection and cDCs were depleted on day 7, 9 and 11, and the number of ESAT-6-specific C7 T cells was determined in mLNs harvested on day 12.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Depletion of classical DCs does not reduce CFU in mLNs of zDC-DTR mice.
claims.source: The number of CFU in mLNs of PBS and DT treated zDC-DTR mice.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E where DT treatment does not reduce mLN CFU.

claims.claim: FLT3L-deficient mice have markedly reduced CD4 T cell responses following Mtb infection.
claims.source: FLT3L-deficient mice, which lack classical DCs but not IMs, also have markedly reduced CD4 T cell responses following Mtb infection (Figure 4F)
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4F by reduced C7 T cell numbers in FLT3L KO mice.

claims.claim: FLT3L-deficient mice lack classical DCs but not IMs.
claims.source: FLT3L-deficient mice, which lack classical DCs but not IMs
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about the FLT3L KO phenotype.

claims.claim: FLT3L-deficient mice have Mtb present in the mLN despite reduced CD4 T cell responses.
claims.source: FLT3L-deficient mice, which lack classical DCs but not IMs, also have markedly reduced CD4 T cell responses following Mtb infection (Figure 4F) despite the presence of Mtb in the mLN (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3 by CFU analysis.

claims.claim: Classical DCs are dispensable for trafficking of live Mtb from infected lungs to mLNs.
claims.source: These results indicate that classical DCs, while dispensable for trafficking of live Mtb from infected lungs to mLNs, are essential for CD4 T cell priming.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the zDC-DTR and FLT3L KO experiments showing normal CFU in mLNs despite DC depletion.

claims.claim: Classical DCs are essential for CD4 T cell priming during Mtb infection.
claims.source: These results indicate that classical DCs, while dispensable for trafficking of live Mtb from infected lungs to mLNs, are essential for CD4 T cell priming.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data from zDC-DTR and FLT3L KO experiments showing reduced T cell responses.

claims.claim: During the second week of murine infection, IMs play the critical role of delivering live Mtb to draining mLNs.
claims.source: During the second week of murine infection, IMs play the critical role of delivering live Mtb to draining mLNs, an indispensable step for Mtb-specific CD4 T cell priming.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion supported by depletion and transfer experiments.

claims.claim: Delivery of live Mtb to draining mLNs is an indispensable step for Mtb-specific CD4 T cell priming.
claims.source: During the second week of murine infection, IMs play the critical role of delivering live Mtb to draining mLNs, an indispensable step for Mtb-specific CD4 T cell priming.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from experiments showing that preventing Mtb delivery to mLNs reduces T cell priming.

claims.claim: IMs serve as transporters of live bacteria from the site of infection to the site of T cell priming.
claims.source: Our results extend previous reports that IMs influence CD4 T cell priming (Leon et al., 2007; Hohl et al., 2009; Nakano et al., 2009; Rivera et al., 2011) by demonstrating that IMs serve as transporters of live bacteria from the site of infection to the site of T cell priming.
claims.evidence: This is the main finding supported by experimental data and extends prior work.

claims.claim: IMs differentiate into DCs in some disease models and directly prime CD4 T cells.
claims.source: In contrast to reports from other disease models demonstrating that IMs differentiate into DCs and then directly prime CD4 T cells (Cheong et al., 2010; Zigmond et al., 2012)
claims.evidence: This refers to findings from other studies supported by citations.

claims.claim: IMs do not prime Mtb-specific CD4 T cells in vivo despite acquiring characteristics of DCs.
claims.source: our adoptive transfer studies using MHC class II KO mice reveal that IMs, despite acquiring characteristics of DCs, do not prime Mtb-specific CD4 T cells in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion from the MHC II transfer experiments shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: moDCs generated in vitro can stimulate T cell responses.
claims.source: Evidence that moDCs generated in vitro can stimulate T cell responses suggests that IMs can process and present antigen (Schreurs et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: IMs can process and present antigen.
claims.source: Evidence that moDCs generated in vitro can stimulate T cell responses suggests that IMs can process and present antigen (Schreurs et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from in vitro studies cited.

claims.claim: Several hundred adoptively transferred IMs were recovered from the mLNs of infected mice.
claims.source: Recovery of several hundred adoptively transferred IMs from the mLNs of infected mice also suggests that sufficient numbers of IM were present to prime T cells.
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental observations from the transfer studies.

claims.claim: IMs infected with Mtb may be ineffective at stimulating Mtb-specific lymphocytes, in contrast to uninfected resident dendritic cells.
claims.source: One possible explanation is that IMs, by virtue of being infected with Mtb, are ineffective at stimulating Mtb-specific lymphocytes, in contrast to resident dendritic cells that have not been infected (Wolf et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the findings, supported by citation.

claims.claim: Multiple DC subsets can be involved in priming of naive T cells.
claims.source: A number of studies, however, have demonstrated that multiple DC subsets can be involved in priming of naive T cells (Itano et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claims.claim: CD103+ DCs play a role in transport and priming during CD8 T cell responses to cutaneous viral infection.
claims.source: Other studies characterizing CD8 T cell responses to cutaneous viral infection have demonstrated a role for CD103+ DCs in transport and priming with potential contributions by inflammatory monocytes (Bedoui et al., 2009; Edismo et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: IMs carry fungal antigens from a site of cutaneous inoculation to draining LNs and transfer antigens to LN resident DCs.
claims.source: One previous study has suggested that IMs carry fungal antigens from a site of cutaneous inoculation to draining LNs and transfer antigens to LN resident DCs (Ersland et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: IMs transport bacteria to lymph nodes and transfer antigen to classical dendritic cells prior to CD4 T cell priming during Mtb infection.
claims.source: Our study extends this finding to live pulmonary infection with Mtb. IMs transport bacteria to lymph nodes and transfer antigen to classical dendritic cells prior to CD4 T cell priming.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study supported by experimental data.

claims.claim: Cross-dressing may play a role during Mtb infection.
claims.source: It is possible that cross-dressing (Wakim et al., 2011), in which infected cells pass MHC molecules to uninfected cells, plays a role during Mtb infection.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about a possible mechanism, with citation.

claims.claim: Transfer of MHC class II molecules from host cells to adoptively transferred, MHC class II-deficient monocytes was not detected.
claims.source: We did not detect transfer of MHC class II molecules from host cells to adoptively transferred, MHC class II-deficient monocytes.
claims.evidence: This is a negative finding from experimental observations.

claims.claim: The number of MHC/peptide complexes required per APC to stimulate T cell responses may be very small and below the level of detection.
claims.source: The number of MHC/peptide complexes required per APC to stimulate T cell responses, however, may be very small and below our level of detection.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on established immunological knowledge.

claims.claim: Transfer of MHC class II molecules in either direction plays a minimal role in T cell priming during Mtb infection.
claims.source: That said, given our finding that MHC class II-deficient IMs effectively complemented monocyte-depleted, MHC class II sufficient mice while MHC class II-expressing monocytes could not correct deficient T cell priming in MHC class II-deficient, monocyte-depleted mice, we believe that transfer of MHC class II molecules in either direction plays a minimal role in T cell priming during Mtb infection.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results with MHC II transfer experiments.

claims.claim: Classical DCs in lymph nodes and their progenitors express the cDC-specific transcription factor zbtb46.
claims.source: Classical DCs in lymph nodes and their progenitors express the cDC-specific transcription factor zbtb46, whereas IMs do not.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about DC markers.

claims.claim: IMs do not express the cDC-specific transcription factor zbtb46.
claims.source: Classical DCs in lymph nodes and their progenitors express the cDC-specific transcription factor zbtb46, whereas IMs do not.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about IM phenotype.

claims.claim: DT administration to zDC-DTR mice leads to a loss of classical DC populations.
claims.source: To determine whether classical DCs are required for Mtb-specific CD4 T cell priming, we used zDC-DTR mice, in which DT administration leads to a loss of classical DC populations (Meredith et al., 2012a; Meredith et al., 2012b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations describing the zDC-DTR mouse model.

claims.claim: M. tuberculosis Erdman was grown in 7H9 media.
claims.source: M. tuberculosis Erdman was grown in 7H9 media, and log phase cultures were diluted to 8 × 106 bacilli per millimeter and sonicated before infection with an aerosol exposure system (Glass-Col).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claims.claim: Aerosol infection was calibrated to deliver approximately 100 CFU per animal.
claims.source: The volume of suspension, and exposure time were calibrated to deliver ∼100 CFU per animal.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claims.claim: Inflammatory monocytes were harvested from the bone marrow of CCR2-GFP mice for adoptive transfer experiments.
claims.source: Inflammatory monocytes were harvested from the bone marrow of CCR2-GFP mice.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claims.claim: 2 × 10^6 purified IMs per mouse were injected via the tail vein for adoptive transfer.
claims.source: The cells were re-suspended in PBS and 2 × 10 (Kipnis et al., 2003) cells per mouse were injected via the tail vein.
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

results.result: Transient depletion of inflammatory monocytes (IMs) during days 7-11 of Mtb infection prevents bacterial delivery to mediastinal lymph nodes (mLNs), reduces CD4 T cell responses in mLNs and lungs, and increases pulmonary bacterial burden.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4 and C21-C27 provide converging evidence from DT-mediated depletion experiments in CCR2-DTR mice. The data show reduced CFU in mLNs (C22), decreased total and CD4 T cell counts (C23-C24), reduced antigen-specific T cells (C25-C26), and increased lung bacterial burden (C27), all supporting the conclusion that IMs are required for bacterial transport and subsequent T cell priming.

results.result: Adoptive transfer of highly purified (>99%) IMs to monocyte-depleted mice restores Mtb delivery to mLNs and rescues CD4 T cell responses, with transferred IMs acquiring DC-like characteristics including expression of CD11c, MHC II, and CD103.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C35 describe a rigorous purification strategy that eliminates contaminating cell types (C29-C31) and demonstrate functional rescue of both bacterial transport (C34) and T cell priming (C35). The acquisition of DC markers by transferred IMs (C33) is well-documented by flow cytometry. This complementation experiment strongly supports the role of IMs in bacterial transport.

results.result: CCR2 signaling is not required for IM trafficking from lungs to mLNs during Mtb infection, as CCR2-deficient and wild-type IMs deliver equivalent amounts of bacteria to mLNs.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C37 are supported by direct comparison experiments showing equivalent CFU delivery by WT and CCR2 KO IMs (Figure 3F). This finding clarifies that while CCR2 is required for bone marrow egress, it is dispensable for trafficking between lung and lymph node during infection.

results.result: IMs do not directly prime Mtb-specific CD4 T cells despite acquiring DC characteristics. Transfer of MHC II-expressing IMs to MHC II-deficient hosts restores bacterial transport but not T cell priming, while MHC II-deficient IMs rescue T cell priming in MHC II-sufficient hosts.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C7, C38-C40, C52, and C64 provide complementary evidence from reciprocal MHC II transfer experiments. The key finding that MHC II+ IMs cannot prime T cells in MHC II KO hosts (C6, C38) while MHC II- IMs rescue priming in MHC II+ hosts (C7, C40) strongly argues against direct antigen presentation by IMs and supports an antigen transfer model. The logic is internally consistent and well-controlled.

results.result: Classical dendritic cells (cDCs) are essential for CD4 T cell priming but dispensable for Mtb transport to mLNs. Depletion of cDCs in zDC-DTR mice or genetic absence in FLT3L-deficient mice markedly reduces T cell responses without affecting bacterial delivery to lymph nodes.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C9 and C41-C47 provide strong evidence from two independent genetic systems (zDC-DTR and FLT3L KO mice) showing dissociation between bacterial transport (maintained) and T cell priming (impaired) when cDCs are absent. The convergent results from different models strengthen the conclusion that cDCs are the critical antigen-presenting cells for T cell priming.

results.result: During the second week of Mtb infection, IMs transport live bacteria from lungs to mLNs where they transfer antigen to classical DCs, which then prime CD4 T cells. This represents a division of labor where IMs serve as bacterial transporters while cDCs function as the actual antigen-presenting cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C11 and C48-C50, C60 synthesize the major findings into a coherent model. The conclusion is well-supported by the combined depletion, transfer, and MHC II experiments showing that both IMs (for transport) and cDCs (for priming) are required but perform distinct functions. This represents the central mechanistic insight of the manuscript.

results.result: The mechanism of antigen transfer from IMs to cDCs remains undefined. Cross-dressing (MHC molecule transfer) was not detected, though the authors acknowledge detection limits may preclude observing small numbers of transferred MHC/peptide complexes.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C64 acknowledge that the molecular mechanism of antigen transfer is unresolved. While C62 reports negative data for MHC transfer, C63 appropriately notes detection limitations. The authors conclude MHC transfer plays a minimal role (C64) based on the reciprocal transfer experiments, but the actual mechanism remains speculative and requires future investigation.

results.result: Background context establishing that CD4 T cells mediate defense against Mtb, IMs express CCR2/Ly6c/CD11b and have been implicated in T cell responses during various infections, and prior CCR2-deficient mouse studies had limitations in temporally defining IM roles.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C12-C19 provide established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations. These claims accurately represent prior work and establish the rationale for using CCR2-DTR mice to achieve temporal control of IM depletion, addressing limitations of constitutive CCR2 knockout models.

results.result: Methodological approaches include use of CCR2-DTR mice for temporal IM depletion, rigorous IM purification excluding NK cells, CD4 T cells, DC progenitors and stem cells (>99% purity), aerosol Mtb infection (~100 CFU), and adoptive transfer of 2×10^6 purified IMs.
results.evaluation: Claims C20, C28-C31, and C68-C71 describe methodological details that are well-documented and appropriate. The IM purification strategy (C29-C31) is particularly rigorous, addressing potential confounding from other CCR2+ cell types (C28). The methods are sufficiently detailed and the purification strategy is validated by FACS data showing >99% purity.

results.result: Discussion of prior literature showing that in some disease models IMs differentiate into DCs and directly prime T cells, that in vitro-generated moDCs can stimulate T cells, and that IMs have been shown to transport fungal antigens to lymph nodes in other infection models.
results.evaluation: Claims C51, C53-C59 accurately represent prior literature with appropriate citations. These claims provide important context for interpreting the current findings, particularly the contrast with other disease models where IMs directly prime T cells (C51) versus the current finding that they do not during Mtb infection (addressed in other result groups).

results.result: Classical DCs and their progenitors express the transcription factor zbtb46 while IMs do not, and zDC-DTR mice enable specific depletion of classical DC populations upon DT administration.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C67 describe established characteristics of the zDC-DTR mouse model supported by appropriate citations (C67). This provides the rationale for using this model to specifically deplete cDCs without affecting IMs, enabling the dissection of their respective roles.

results.result: Transient depletion of inflammatory monocytes during early Mtb infection prevents bacterial delivery to mediastinal lymph nodes and reduces CD4 T cell priming, demonstrating that IMs play a critical role in transporting live Mtb from lungs to lymph nodes during the second week of infection.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe this as an 'elegant and straightforward study' and explicitly state it 'makes an important contribution on the role of different APCs in transport and presentation of antigen in vivo.' The core finding that IMs transport bacteria to lymph nodes is accepted without challenge.

results.result: MHC class II transfer experiments demonstrate that inflammatory monocytes transport Mtb to lymph nodes but do not directly prime CD4 T cells; instead, they transfer antigen to classical dendritic cells that perform the priming function.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this as a 'major conclusion of the study' without challenging the experimental design or interpretation. They note this finding distinguishes the study from other disease models where monocytes directly prime T cells, indicating acceptance of the conclusion.

results.result: Classical dendritic cells are dispensable for Mtb transport to lymph nodes but essential for CD4 T cell priming, as shown by depletion experiments using zDC-DTR mice and FLT3L-deficient mice.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding as part of the study's contribution to understanding 'the role of different APCs in transport and presentation of antigen.' The complementary roles of IMs and cDCs are not questioned, indicating reviewer acceptance.

results.result: Adoptively transferred inflammatory monocytes acquire DC-like characteristics, engraft in lungs and lymph nodes, restore Mtb delivery and T cell responses in depleted mice, demonstrating their function as bacterial transporters.
results.evaluation: Reviewers describe the study as 'elegant and straightforward' without raising concerns about the adoptive transfer methodology or interpretation. The rescue experiments are implicitly accepted as supporting the main conclusions.

results.result: The mechanism by which inflammatory monocytes fail to prime T cells despite acquiring DC characteristics remains unclear, with possible explanations including infection-induced dysfunction or cross-dressing of MHC molecules.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly identify this as 'the only open aspect' and request insights on 'why the monocytes that carry Mtb to lymph nodes do not present antigen to CD4+ T cells.' They suggest several mechanistic possibilities but note these experiments are 'not essential to support the major conclusions.'

results.result: Highly purified inflammatory monocytes (>99% pure) were isolated using a strategy that eliminates other CCR2-expressing cells, and CCR2 signaling is not required for IM trafficking between lungs and lymph nodes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not question the purification strategy or the specificity of the depletion approach. The acceptance of the main conclusions implicitly validates these methodological controls.

results.result: Background context establishing that CCR2+ inflammatory monocytes have been implicated in immune responses to various infections including Mtb, though their specific in vivo contribution during Mtb infection remained unresolved.
results.evaluation: These are background claims establishing context and prior knowledge. Reviewers do not challenge these statements and they frame the rationale for the study's investigation.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect alignment on background claims (C1-C2, C12-C19). Both evaluations support these as established context and prior knowledge without challenge. OpenEval emphasizes the rationale for CCR2-DTR mice, while peer reviewers accept the framing without question.

Strong agreement on MHC II transfer experiments (C5-C7, C38-C40, C52, C64). Both evaluations support the conclusion that IMs do not directly prime T cells but transfer antigen to cDCs. Peer reviewers describe this as a 'major conclusion' accepted without challenge, while OpenEval notes the logic is 'internally consistent and well-controlled.'

Strong agreement on cDC requirement for T cell priming (C8-C9, C41-C47). Both evaluations support the dissociation between bacterial transport (maintained) and T cell priming (impaired) when cDCs are depleted. Peer reviewers accept this as part of understanding 'different APCs in transport and presentation,' while OpenEval emphasizes convergent results from independent genetic systems.

Strong agreement on IM depletion experiments (C3-C4, C21-C27). Both evaluations support the conclusion that IMs are required for bacterial transport and T cell priming. Peer reviewers describe the study as 'elegant and straightforward' and accept the core finding, while OpenEval notes 'converging evidence' from multiple experimental readouts. Peer review also includes C48-C49 in this grouping.

Perfect agreement on uncertainty regarding antigen transfer mechanism (C61-C63). Both evaluations mark this as UNCERTAIN. Peer reviewers explicitly identify this as 'the only open aspect' and request mechanistic insights, while OpenEval notes the mechanism 'remains speculative and requires future investigation.' Both acknowledge C64's conclusion about minimal MHC transfer role.

Partial overlap on IM adoptive transfer experiments (C29-C35). Both evaluations support these claims. OpenEval emphasizes the rigorous purification strategy and functional rescue of both transport and priming, while peer reviewers implicitly accept the methodology by describing the study as 'elegant' without raising concerns. Peer review groups these with C10-C11, C50.

Partial overlap on the integrated model (C10-C11, C50). Both evaluations support the conclusion that IMs and cDCs perform distinct but complementary functions. OpenEval synthesizes this as 'the central mechanistic insight,' while peer reviewers accept it as part of the overall contribution. Peer review also includes adoptive transfer claims (C32-C35) in this grouping.

Partial overlap on CCR2 independence for trafficking (C36-C37). Both evaluations support these claims. OpenEval emphasizes the direct comparison showing CCR2 is dispensable for lung-to-lymph node trafficking, while peer reviewers implicitly accept this through their validation of methodological controls. Peer review also includes purification strategy claims (C29-C31) in this grouping.

Partial overlap on methodological details (C29-C31). Both evaluations support the rigorous IM purification strategy. OpenEval provides detailed validation noting >99% purity and addresses confounding from other CCR2+ cells (C20, C28, C68-C71), while peer reviewers implicitly accept the methodology without questioning the purification approach.

Minimal overlap (C56 only). OpenEval evaluates C51, C53-C59 as SUPPORTED background literature providing context for interpreting findings. Peer review R5 focuses on the unresolved mechanism (C56, C61-C63) and marks it UNCERTAIN. The evaluations address different aspects with little substantive overlap.

OpenEval evaluates zDC-DTR mouse model characteristics (C65-C67) as SUPPORTED background with appropriate citations. No corresponding peer review evaluation found; peer reviewers did not separately evaluate these methodological background claims.
